content.title: About
content.content: Beef tenderloin is a lean, buttery‑textured cut taken from the lumbar region of the cow. It is prized for its tenderness, low fat content, and rich beef flavor. Tenderloin is commonly used for steaks because it cooks quickly and stays juicy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tenderloin is the most tender beef cut, often compared to chicken breast in softness.
It is traditionally cooked on a grill or in a hot skillet to highlight its natural flavor.
Different countries have their own names: in the US it’s called “tenderloin steak,” in France “filet de bœuf.”
For the perfect steak, let the tenderloin sit at room temperature for 30‑40 minutes before cooking.
Beef tenderloin is high in protein and iron but low in connective tissue.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Tenderloin provides about 22 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Tenderloin has one of the lowest fat levels among beef cuts, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are essential for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Creatine and carnosine
items.content: These compounds help improve physical performance and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although lean, tenderloin still contains cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens such as E. coli. Cook steaks to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals can have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Beef is high in purines, which can exacerbate gout symptoms in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tenderloin is best cooked over high heat: grilling, pan‑searing, or broiling. Season with salt and pepper, sear each side for a few minutes, then let rest 5‑10 minutes so juices redistribute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tenderloin in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or an airtight container, for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag; it will keep well for up to 6 months.
